cards.front: Name the four jobs an AI assistant does well.
cards.back: Drafting new text, summarising long text, reformatting text into a new shape, and brainstorming options.

cards.front: An answer that sounds right but is made up is called a ____.
cards.back: Hallucination. It is the main reason you check facts, figures and sources from an assistant.

cards.front: Name four things an AI assistant is unreliable at.
cards.back: Facts with no source, maths, recent events, and anything it cannot see, such as your inbox or private team files.

cards.front: You ask an assistant for last quarter's total refunds. It replies with a precise figure. What should you conclude?
cards.back: Treat it as invented unless the assistant was connected to the refunds system. It cannot see your data by default, so take the figure from the finance report instead.

cards.front: What do the letters RTCF stand for in a prompt?
cards.back: Role, Task, Context and Format: who the assistant acts as, what exactly to do, the background and constraints, and the shape of the output.

cards.front: In RTCF, the part that sets the shape of the output, such as five bullets or a 100-word email, is the ____.
cards.back: Format. It tells the assistant how long the reply should be and how to lay it out.

cards.front: Which RTCF element is missing? Draft a reply to a customer asking about delivery times, for a frustrated first-time buyer, in under 120 words.
cards.back: Role. Task, context and format are present, so add who the assistant should act as, for example a friendly customer service specialist.

cards.front: The first draft is too formal and too long. What is the best next step?
cards.back: Iterate. Reply with a specific change, such as: make it friendlier and cut it to 80 words. This is faster than writing a new prompt.

cards.front: Which four kinds of detail must you always check in AI output?
cards.back: Names, numbers, quotes and links. Each one can look convincing while being wrong.

cards.front: Checking a sample of items when a full check is impractical is called ____.
cards.back: Spot-checking. Still check every item that would cause harm if wrong.

cards.front: An AI summary quotes your chief executive and gives a link as its source. What do you do before using the quote?
cards.back: Open the link and find the exact words. If the page does not contain them, remove the quote or replace it with one you have confirmed.

cards.front: List five kinds of data that must never go into an unapproved AI tool.
cards.back: Personal data, customer records, passwords or keys, confidential financials, and legal matters.

cards.front: Replacing names and identifying details with placeholders such as Customer A is called ____.
cards.back: Anonymising. Remove every detail that could identify a person, not only the name.

cards.front: A colleague pastes an employee's sick-leave record into a free public chatbot to draft a return-to-work letter. What should they have done?
cards.back: Use the approved enterprise assistant, and anonymise the request anyway. Health details are especially sensitive, so describe the situation in general terms and add specifics afterwards.

cards.front: Name the four signs of a good AI use case.
cards.back: High volume, low risk, easy to verify, and you have the expertise to judge the output.

cards.front: Which is the better first use case for an HR team: drafting interview invitation emails or ranking candidates for a shortlist?
cards.back: Drafting invitations. They are frequent, low risk and easy to check. Ranking candidates is a decision about people and must stay with a person.

cards.front: A task saves 30 minutes a week but needs 35 minutes of checking. Is it a good use case?
cards.back: No. It loses five minutes a week once checking is counted. Choose tasks where the net saving is clearly positive.

cards.front: Complete the rule: the assistant drafts, ____ decides.
cards.back: You. You own everything you send, sign or act on, whoever wrote the first version.

cards.front: Name four situations where you should escalate AI-assisted work before it goes out.
cards.back: Legal exposure, large sums of money, safety risks, and decisions about a person. In each case a manager or specialist should review it first.

cards.front: An AI-drafted reply to a client accepts a penalty clause. You are unsure whether that is allowed. What do you do?
cards.back: Do not send it. Escalate to your manager or the legal team, because the reply creates a legal commitment. Send only the approved version, under your own name.
